summary: Describes the X.500 directory information models as used in LDAP, which define how directory entries, attributes and schema are structured. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: The blueprint for how an address book is arranged: what an entry is, what facts it holds, and how entries are filed.

questions: what is the ldap information model
what is a distinguished name in ldap
what are structural and auxiliary object classes
subtitle: How LDAP thinks about a directory: a tree of entries, typed attributes, and a schema that servers publish about themselves.

tldr.problem: LDAP gives access to X.500-style directories, but clients and servers need a shared picture of what a directory holds, how entries are named, and how the rules about them are described.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4512 adapts the X.500 information models for LDAP. Entries form a tree (the DIT), each entry is a set of attributes governed by object classes, and schema definitions plus a server's own capabilities are readable as operational attributes.
tldr.outcome: It replaces large parts of RFC 2251, RFC 2252 and RFC 2256 and all of RFC 3674, and became the model part of the LDAP technical specification.

today: RFC 4512 is a Proposed Standard from June 2006, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes parts of RFC 2251, RFC 2252 and RFC 2256, and all of RFC 3674.

sections.title: The Directory and Its Two Models
sections.content:
RFC 4512 describes the X.500 Directory Information Models as the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) uses them. The Directory is a collection of open systems cooperating to provide directory services, and the information it holds is the Directory Information Base (DIB). A user reaches it through a client (a Directory User Agent), which talks to one or more servers (Directory System Agents, or DSAs). Each server holds a fragment of the DIB.

The DIB holds two classes of information: user information, provided and administered by users, and administrative and operational information, used to run the directory. These two generic models are the framework for the rest of the document, which also covers the subschema model and the server (DSA) informational model.

The RFC includes material from X.501, adapted for LDAP, and says those adaptations apply only to this protocol. Its scope within the LDAP specification set is explained in the final section.
sections.plainLanguage: A directory is a big shared address book kept in many places. It holds the facts people care about, and also private notes the book keeps to run itself.

sections.title: Entries, Attributes and the Tree
sections.content:
A directory entry is a named collection of information and the basic unit the Directory holds. An object entry represents a particular object, an alias entry provides alternative naming, and a subentry holds administrative or operational information. Entries are organized as a tree, the Directory Information Tree (DIT). If an arc runs from X to Y, X is the immediate superior (parent) of Y and Y its immediate subordinate (child).

An entry is a set of attributes. An attribute is an attribute description (a type plus zero or more options) with one or more values. The attribute type decides whether it can be multi-valued and which syntax and matching rules apply. No two values of an attribute may be equivalent under its equality matching rule. For example, a givenName attribute cannot hold both "John" and "JOHN".

Attribute descriptions are written like cn;lang-de;lang-en. The option order is irrelevant and all attributes of an entry must have distinct descriptions. The RFC also allows hierarchies of descriptions, so that asking for a general description such as name also finds values stored under a more specific one such as cn.
sections.plainLanguage: The directory is like a family tree of cards. Each card lists facts, such as a name or a phone number, and the cards hang from other cards in a tree.

sections.title: Naming Entries and Aliases
sections.content:
Each entry is named relative to its parent by a Relative Distinguished Name (RDN): an unordered set of one or more attribute value assertions, each an attribute description with zero options and a value. An RDN must be unique among siblings. The RFC's examples are UID=12345, OU=Engineering and the multi-valued CN=Kurt Zeilenga+L=Redwood Shores.

An entry's full name, its Distinguished Name (DN), is its RDN joined to its parent's DN, for example UID=nobody@example.com,DC=example,DC=com. A DN unambiguously refers to one entry.

An alias entry gives an object a second name. It belongs to the alias object class and holds an aliasedObjectName attribute naming the target. Converting an alias to the real name is called dereferencing, and an alias entry is always a leaf with no subordinates.
sections.plainLanguage: Each card has a short label that is unique among its siblings. Put the labels from the top of the tree down to the card and you get its full address. An alias is a sign that says "see that other card".

sections.title: Object Classes
sections.content:
An object class is a family of objects that share characteristics. Each class lists the attributes an entry must have (MUST) and may have (MAY), and a subclass inherits those from its superclasses. Classes can have more than one direct superclass. Every entry belongs to the abstract class top, defined as ( 2.5.6.0 NAME 'top' ABSTRACT MUST objectClass ).

There are three kinds. Abstract classes only supply a base to inherit from. Structural classes describe the real-world object, and each object or alias entry has exactly one structural class, which shall not be changed. Auxiliary classes add attributes and can be added to or removed from an entry over time, but only those the governing DIT content rule allows.

The objectClass attribute lists an entry's classes. When a class is added, its superclasses are implicitly added, and servers must prevent deleting a superclass of a remaining value. Servers following X.500(93) models must also stop the basic structural class changing, so one cannot change a person into a country.
sections.plainLanguage: Object classes are like job descriptions. "Person" says you need a name, while an extra badge, such as "has a mailbox", can be added later for more fields.

sections.title: Schema Definitions
sections.content:
The Directory schema is the set of rules about what the tree can contain. It prevents, for instance, a country below a person, a serial number on a person entry, or a value of the wrong syntax. It is made of name forms, DIT structure rules, DIT content rules, object classes, attribute types, matching rules and, in LDAP, LDAP syntaxes.

Each kind has a text description format written in ABNF and starting with an object identifier (OID), optionally with NAME short names, DESC and OBSOLETE. Object classes add SUP, a kind and MUST/MAY, and the default kind is STRUCTURAL. Attribute types add fields such as EQUALITY, ORDERING, SUBSTR, SYNTAX, SINGLE-VALUE, NO-USER-MODIFICATION and USAGE. A bound in curly braces after the syntax, as in 1.3.6.4.1.1466.0{64}, suggests a minimum upper bound on length, not part of the syntax name.

DIT content rules extend an entry's allowed attributes and auxiliary classes, and can preclude attributes with NOT. DIT structure rules and name forms control where entries sit in the tree and which attributes form their RDNs. Servers MAY support these rules.
sections.plainLanguage: The schema is the rulebook for the address book. It stops you from writing a shoe size in the phone number box, and it is written in a strict, tidy format.

sections.title: Operational Information and Subschema Discovery
sections.content:
Some attributes are operational attributes, kept by servers for administration. They are not returned in search results unless requested by name, and not all are user-modifiable. Servers SHOULD maintain four of them for every entry: creatorsName, createTimestamp, modifiersName and modifyTimestamp. The RFC also defines structuralObjectClass and governingStructureRule.

Schema lives in a subschema (sub)entry, which belongs to the subschema auxiliary class and holds attributes such as objectClasses, attributeTypes, matchingRules, matchingRuleUse, dITContentRules, dITStructureRules and nameForms. A server that masters modifiable entries SHALL provide a subschemaSubentry attribute in each, so clients can discover which attributes and classes are permitted.

To discover schema, a client reads an entry's subschemaSubentry, then searches that DN with scope baseObject and filter (objectClass=subschema), naming the schema attributes it wants. Clients SHOULD NOT assume a published subschema is complete.
sections.plainLanguage: The book keeps secret notes, like who wrote each card and when. To learn the rules of the book, you look up the card that holds the rulebook.

sections.title: The Server Informational Model
sections.content:
LDAP assumes one or more servers jointly provide a DIT. The server holding the original information is the master; servers with copies are shadowing or caching servers. A naming context is the largest collection of entries starting at an entry mastered by one server, including subordinates down to entries mastered elsewhere. Its context prefix is the name of the initial entry.

Each server describes itself in the root DSE, the entry whose DN has zero RDNs (the zero-length string). A client reads it with a Search using an empty baseObject, scope baseObject and filter (objectClass=*), naming the attributes wanted. Its attributes are operational, and it is not included in a subtree search from the root.

  • altServer: alternative servers to try;
  • namingContexts: the naming contexts the server masters or shadows;
  • supportedControl, supportedExtension, supportedFeatures: recognized controls, extended operations and features;
  • supportedLDAPVersion: LDAP versions supported;
  • supportedSASLMechanisms: recognized SASL mechanisms, which may depend on session state.

Servers that cache or shadow entries answer searches and comparisons but refer modifications elsewhere, and MUST NOT violate the access controls of the originating server.
sections.plainLanguage: Every library branch has a front desk card that says what the branch has and what it can do. You ask the front desk first, before asking for anything else.

sections.title: Implementation Guidelines and Cautions
sections.content:
Servers MUST recognize the names of all attribute types and object classes this document defines, though they need not support the functionality. They MUST ensure entries conform to schema rules. Support for DIT content rules, DIT structure rules, name forms, alias entries, extensibleObject and subentries is optional (MAY). Servers SHOULD publish all schema elements they support in subschema entries.

Clients SHOULD NOT assume any schema elements beyond those baseline ones without prior agreement, and should read the subschema. Clients MUST NOT decode a value as ASN.1 if its syntax is unknown, and MUST NOT assume the string encoding is limited to UTF-8 text or any subset of Unicode unless stated.

Short names (descriptors) are only aliases for OIDs. The same short name can mean different things in different subschemas, or even refer to both an object class and an attribute type in one subschema, so implementations MUST be prepared for that.

On security, the RFC notes only that entry attributes can describe people, organizations or devices, that most countries have privacy laws about publishing information on people, and that RFC 4511 and RFC 4513 cover access security. IANA updated the LDAP descriptors registry for the names defined here.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers should be ready to understand the standard card types. Clients should ask what a server knows instead of guessing, and be careful with other people's private details.
